o: We must read `file.txt` where every row has the same number of space-separated fields and print the matrix transpose: row *i* of the output contains field *i* from every input row. In the example, the first column (`name`, `alice`, `ryan`) becomes output row 1 and the second column becomes output row 2. Since all rows have equal length, we can either collect columns while streaming lines or read everything into memory and index by position. The main pitfalls are handling trailing whitespace/newlines and joining fields with single spaces without a trailing separator.
k: Transposing means output row i = column i of the input; with fixed row lengths this is just an index swap.
Streaming with awk avoids storing the whole file: accumulate each column into its own buffer.
Join fields with a single space and avoid trailing spaces when printing each output line.

a.n: Approach 1: Read all rows into memory and transpose by indexing
a.i: Read every line, split on spaces, and store rows in a list. The answer's row i is formed by taking element i from every stored row. This directly mirrors the mathematical definition of a transpose and works because all rows have the same number of columns.
s: Read all lines of file.txt, strip newline characters.
Split each line on spaces to get a list of fields.
For each column index j, build a line by collecting fields[j] from every row.
Print each built line joined by single spaces.

c.python:
with open('file.txt') as f:
    rows = [line.split() for line in f if line.strip()]
for j in range(len(rows[0])):
    print(' '.join(row[j] for row in rows))

a.t: O(R x C) — every field is read once and printed once.
a.sp: O(R x C) — the entire file is held in memory.

a.n: Approach 2: Streaming with awk (optimal shell idiom)
a.i: awk processes the file line by line. For each line, append each field to the buffer for its column, separating accumulated values with a space. At the end, print all column buffers — this produces the transpose without ever storing a 2-D structure.
s: For each input line, loop over its NF fields.
Append field i to buffer[i], prefixing a space if the buffer is non-empty.
After processing all lines (END block), print each buffer on its own line.
a.t: O(R x C) — each field is appended to exactly one column buffer.
a.sp: O(R x C) worst case for buffers, but no explicit 2-D grid of rows is kept; in pure awk this is the canonical one-pass solution.

w: In an interview (or on LeetCode's Shell judge), prefer the awk-style streaming approach — it is idiomatic, one pass, and easy to explain. Approach 1 is fine when memory is not a concern and is easier to get right quickly. Common pitfalls: printing a trailing space after the last field (use conditional separators), mishandling empty/trailing lines, and forgetting that split behavior differs across languages (awk splits on runs of whitespace automatically). Edge cases: a single-row file (output is one column, one word per line) and a single-column file (output is one line). Follow-ups may ask how to handle ragged rows (pad with empty fields) or very large files that exceed memory — the streaming approach already addresses the latter.
